m6s1p1: A solar system is a long-term investment designed to operate for 25–30 years. Without regular maintenance, energy yield degrades much faster than the manufacturer's warranty assumes. Dust, dirt, bird droppings and leaf deposits on the panel surface can reduce output by 10–30 % depending on climate and location.
m6s1p2: Beyond soiling, the system's electrical connections, mounting hardware and inverter components are exposed to weather and thermal cycling year-round. Proactive inspection catches small problems — a loose connector, a cracked bypass diode, a corroding terminal — before they become costly failures or safety hazards.
m6s1callout: Industry data shows that a well-maintained residential system degrades at roughly 0.5 % per year, while a neglected system can degrade at 1–2 % per year. Over 25 years, the cumulative difference in energy production can exceed 15 %.
m6s2p1: Panel cleaning frequency depends on local conditions. In dry, dusty climates (desert regions, near farmland or construction sites) monthly cleaning may be necessary. In wetter, windier climates with regular rainfall, quarterly cleaning is often sufficient — rain acts as a natural rinse.
m6s2p2: Always clean panels in the early morning or late afternoon when they are cool. Applying cold water to hot panels can cause thermal shock and micro-cracks. Use soft-bristle brushes or squeegees with de-ionised or low-mineral water to avoid leaving mineral deposits.
m6s2callout: Never use abrasive pads, high-pressure washers (above 35 bar), or harsh detergents. These can scratch the anti-reflective coating and void the panel warranty. Check your manufacturer's cleaning guidelines before using any cleaning agent.
m6s3p1: A thorough electrical inspection should be performed at least once a year, ideally before peak production season. The checklist covers: panel connectors (MC4 or equivalent) — check for moisture ingress, corrosion and secure seating; string combiner and junction boxes — inspect for overheating marks, insulation damage and correct labelling; DC disconnect and AC breaker — verify operation and torque of terminal screws; battery terminals (if applicable) — clean corrosion with bicarbonate solution, check electrolyte level in flooded lead-acid cells; inverter — review fault log, check cooling fan operation and air filter if present.
m6s3p2: Use a clamp meter to verify that each string's short-circuit current matches the expected value from the datasheet. A string producing significantly less current than its neighbours may have a failed panel, shading issue or a degraded connector.
m6s3callout: DC circuits in solar systems can carry lethal voltage even at night due to charged batteries. Always use appropriate PPE, insulated tools and a voltage tester before touching any DC conductor. Follow local electrical safety regulations.
m6s4p1: Shading is one of the most insidious performance losses because it can be partial, seasonal and hard to detect without monitoring data. A shadow on a single cell reduces the output of the entire string it belongs to if no bypass diodes or power optimisers are present.
m6s4p2: Common shading sources include: trees that have grown since installation, new construction on neighbouring properties, satellite dishes, chimneys, and seasonal changes in the sun's path (the sun is lower in winter, casting longer shadows). Use a solar pathfinder, a smartphone app, or monitoring software to identify shading periods.
m6s4callout: Thermal imaging (thermography) is the gold standard for diagnosing shading and cell defects. A thermal camera reveals hot spots caused by mismatched or damaged cells, allowing targeted replacement before the defect causes fire or connector failure.
m6s5p1: Modern inverters include built-in data loggers accessible via Wi-Fi or a manufacturer's cloud portal. Monitor these key metrics daily: daily energy yield (kWh); specific yield (kWh/kWp) compared to local irradiance data; performance ratio (PR) — ratio of actual to theoretical yield, target > 75 %; inverter operating temperature; string currents and voltages.
m6s5p2: Set up automated alerts for: yield below 80 % of the rolling 30-day average; any inverter fault code; battery state-of-charge below minimum threshold. Early detection of a decline in specific yield — even 5–8 % below baseline — can point to soiling, shading, a failed string or an ageing battery before a major failure occurs.
m6s5callout: Keep a logbook (digital or paper) recording each inspection date, cleaning performed, any faults observed and corrective actions taken. This record is valuable for warranty claims and for tracking long-term system health.
schedMonthlyNote: Dry regions, near farmland or construction sites. Visible soiling accumulates quickly.
schedQuarterlyNote: Regular rainfall helps. Clean before and after wet season for best results.
schedAnnualNote: High rainfall keeps panels relatively clean. Annual inspection still recommended.
m6t1Def: Energy loss due to dirt, dust or debris on the panel surface. Can reach 10–30 % without regular cleaning.
m6t2Def: Annual percentage decline in panel power output. Well-maintained panels degrade at ~0.5 %/year.
m6t3Def: Ratio of actual energy output to theoretical maximum given local irradiance. A healthy system targets PR > 75 %.
m6t4Def: Localised overheating in a cell caused by partial shading or damage. Detectable via thermal imaging.
m6t5Def: Annual energy produced per installed kilowatt-peak (kWh/kWp). The key metric for comparing system performance.
m6t6Def: Diode integrated in the junction box that routes current around a shaded or faulty cell string within the panel.
